They specialize in teaching people how to overcome SA, and teach skills on how to develop interpersonal relationships. If you cannot afford the classes then the books are a good place to start, but I believe the classroom provides actual social interaction in a safe environment vs. trying to learn from a book and then going out the in world and attempting to practice.

On a more serious note, if you need improvement in social skills, public speaking, or, like I was, were looking to overcome a serious speech impediment, I recommend Toastmasters. It is an international nonprofit organization existing for the sole purpose of bettering communication and leadership skills. I know it might sound lame, but I did it for a year at the end of high school. It eliminated my stutter, and took me from the bottom quartile of speakers to making public speaking a strength of mine. It's a serious advantage and a career booster. No matter where you live, there's probably a local group within driving distance of you. Just sit in on a meeting, it's free, and if you decide to try it, totally worth it.
Start striking up conversations with random people out and about. You'll get better and more comfortable with practice. You'll mess up at first but you'll never see them again, so who cares?
Practice your stories. Do interesting things. Know interesting things. Talk to strangers. Teach someone something.

Grab a copy of "Rules of The Game" by Neil Strauss.

It has a 30 day exercise program to help you overcome your SA with strategies for developing social and business skill. Once you build some confidence, you'll have no trouble. Keep you head up, you're a champ!

Start small. "How's your day going?" said in a manner that implies you actually care can get you more than just the typical "good" in response.

Look at the people around you. Are they wearing anything that pertains to an interest of yours? Say you're a baseball fan and you see someone wearing an A's jersey; you have common ground with this person and if they don't look actively busy, a simple "Hey, what'd you think of the game yesterday?" may start something. See someone wearing a shit of a band you like, walk up smile, "Hey, I love those guys!"

Learn the comment-question technique, sometimes called conversation threading. The short version is you make a comment related to what someone just said, then ask them a question about. "Oh, my sister does cross-stitch, too! Do you have any projects you're working on now?"

If you don't have anything to say, don't force it. If it's been more than just a single comment and response, just smile and say "Cool, nice talking to you" and go about your business.

Honestly, for me... one of the biggest things that helped, was just getting more life experience. I went to museums, watched tons of movies accross all genres... musicals, actions, dramas, romantic comedies, old classic films, etc... I expanded my taste in music... jazz, rap, metal, country, etc...

The point was just to know a little bit about everything, so that I would always have something to say. People talking about a movie... I've seen that movie! People talking about a band... I've heard that album!

In the end though, I learned a lot about myself... what I liked, what I didn't like... and knowing more about me, made it easier to talk to others about them.

The only down side is that you have to do things by yourself for awhile... and having anxiety, that can be a bit of a shitty experience. I always felt so bad going to a movie or a museum by myself... but honestly, nobody gave a shit. I always thought they would hate me, maybe think I'm a loser... but really, people just thought I was some guy at a museum, which I was.

Also, sometimes, I would talk to complete strangers for practice. People I would never see again. Not long conversations, just random remarks... like a guy scratching loto tickets outside of 7-11.... "Hey bro, if you win, I call dibs on the first thousand!" -- just shit like that... just to get over my apprehension to speak up.

Oh, and don't think. If you want to say something, say it... and do it quick. The longer you wait, the more you'll convince yourself it's stupid and you won't talk. At some point, just realize that it's better to say anything, then nothing.
